sections.h2: Can a squatter take ownership of a Maryland house?
sections.html:
Only after meeting every element of adverse possession for 20 years, and a court has to agree. A person who simply moves into a vacant house has no ownership claim the day they arrive.

The 20 year number comes from Courts and Judicial Proceedings 5-103(a). It gives a person 20 years from the date the cause of action accrues either to file suit to recover possession of land or to enter the land. After that window the true owner's right to recover is cut off. The statute leaves the common-law doctrine of prescription alone for rights such as easements, and it preserves the limits in Real Property 6-103 and 8-107.

Years of absence create the exposure. A vacant inherited house, a rental left empty after a tenant moved out, or a lot nobody has walked in years are the situations where a claim could grow over time.

sections.h2: What a claimant has to prove
sections.html:
Maryland courts apply three elements: possession that is actual, open, notorious and exclusive; possession that is continuous for the full period; and possession that is hostile and under a claim of title or ownership. Appellate opinions quote this three-part test from Senez v. Collins.

The claimant carries the burden of showing the elements for 20 years. Under Hungerford v. Hungerford, every element must be shown, and if one is missing the possession doesn't give title.

ElementWhat it means for a house
Actual, open, notorious, exclusiveLiving in or openly using the house in a way the owner could see, without sharing control with the owner
Continuous for 20 yearsNo long gaps in use during the period
Hostile, under claim of titleOccupying as if the owner, not with the owner's permission

Permission matters. Someone who stays with the owner's consent, or under a lease, isn't hostile in the legal sense. A written record of who was allowed in can help you later.

The route depends on who the person is. A current or former tenant goes through the landlord-tenant process. Someone with no lease and no right to be there can be removed through a wrongful detainer case or, since October 2025, a sheriff affidavit for fraudulent occupancy.

For tenants and holdovers, the landlord first wins a judgment in a rent court, breach of lease or holding over case, then petitions for a warrant of restitution. A sheriff or constable must be present at the eviction, and it can't happen on a Sunday or a holiday. Owners can't lock out an occupant on their own.

For an unauthorized occupant who is not a tenant, the wrongful detainer action in Real Property 14-132 applies. It is a District Court case for someone holding possession without the right to it. It can't be used against a current tenant, a holdover tenant or someone with a court order protecting their possession.

  • Lease or rent history exists: use the landlord-tenant case and a warrant of restitution.
  • No lease and no permission: consider wrongful detainer.
  • Unsure of the occupant's status: ask a Maryland attorney before acting.

Senate Bill 46 (Chapter 188 of the 2025 laws) took effect October 1, 2025. It created a new crime of fraudulent occupancy and sped up the wrongful detainer process.

Under the new Criminal Law 8-906, it is a misdemeanor to occupy or claim a right to occupy a residence you have no lawful right to, with intent to defraud. A first violation carries up to 90 days in jail, a fine up to $500, or both. A second violation within two years rises to up to six months and $1,000, and later violations within two years of the previous one go up to one year and $2,500.

An owner can file a sworn affidavit with the county sheriff saying a person is fraudulently in possession. The sheriff must then remove that person and return the property, but a deputy may not remove an occupant who shows evidence of lawful possession. The offense doesn't apply where a court order granted possession or where a remedy exists under Title 8 of the Real Property Article, so landlord-tenant disputes stay in court.

The process is faster than it used to be. The same 2025 act set tight deadlines for each step.

StepRule in Chapter 188
SummonsMay be addressed to OCCUPANT LOCATED AT the property address when the name is unknown
HearingNo more than 10 business days after the complaint is filed
ServiceCompleted within 4 business days; after two good-faith attempts on different days, mailing plus posting counts
DefaultCourt must enter a default judgment if the defendant does not attend
AppealDeadline cut from 10 days to 4 days after judgment

The owner still has to show a legal interest in the property. If the court finds the owner entitled to possession, it issues a warrant directing the sheriff to deliver possession immediately. Damages and fees may be awarded if they were claimed in the complaint. Older guides online may mention a 10 day appeal period, which no longer applies.

sections.h2: How an adverse possession claim affects a sale
sections.html:
A claim, or even a rumor of one, clouds title and can stall a closing. Buyers and their title companies will ask who occupies the property and on what basis.

Real Property 14-108 lets a person in peaceable possession, under color of title or claim of right, bring a quiet title action in the circuit court where the land sits. The adverse claim does not have to be actively asserted. A suit of this kind must name anyone who appears of record or who claims a hostile outstanding right. An old boundary dispute or an occupant's claim of ownership can end up before a judge before a clean sale is possible.

Cash Home Buyers works with Maryland sellers who have occupied, inherited or neglected houses, and we buy as-is. If someone is living in a house you own, first find out whether they are a tenant, a guest or an unauthorized occupant, because that decides which court process applies.

  • Keep copies of leases, texts and receipts that show whether the occupant had permission.
  • Photograph the property and record the dates you last inspected it.
  • Pay taxes and keep insurance active on a vacant house.
  • Do not change locks or remove belongings before a court order.

Visit the property regularly, keep records of those visits and act quickly when someone is in the house without permission.

The legislature is still working on the topic. Senate Bill 989 from 2025 proposed a sheriff registry of unauthorized occupants for owners of residential dwellings, with enrollment for six months. Bring your visit log, photographs and any lease or permission records to the first meeting with an attorney or the sheriff's office, since those papers show how long the house was empty and who had a right to be inside. If the house is more trouble than it is worth, selling it as-is for cash ends the exposure.

faqs.q: How long does adverse possession take in Maryland?
faqs.a: The statute sets 20 years from when the owner's cause of action accrues. Courts also require the possession to be continuous and hostile for that full period.

faqs.q: Is a squatter the same as a tenant in Maryland?
faqs.a: No. A tenant has a lease or rental agreement, and the owner removes a tenant through the landlord-tenant court process and a warrant of restitution. An unauthorized occupant with no lease can be the subject of a wrongful detainer case.

faqs.q: Can the sheriff remove a squatter in Maryland?
faqs.a: Yes in some cases. Since October 1, 2025, an owner can file a sworn affidavit of fraudulent occupancy with the county sheriff, but the sheriff may not remove someone who shows evidence of lawful possession.

faqs.q: How fast is wrongful detainer in Maryland?
faqs.a: The hearing must be no more than 10 business days after the complaint is filed, and service must be completed within 4 business days. The appeal deadline is now 4 days.

faqs.q: Can I change the locks on someone living in my house?
faqs.a: No. For tenants, eviction needs a court judgment and a warrant of restitution carried out with the sheriff or constable present.
